title: How the eye works
keyIdea: We see when light gets into our eyes. Light from a lamp or the Sun bounces off things and goes in through the pupil, a hole in the coloured iris. The lens bends the light so a sharp picture lands on the retina at the back of the eye. The retina sends a message along the optic nerve, and the brain works out what we are looking at. The iris makes the pupil small in bright light and big in the dark.
familyTip: Stand by a mirror in a dim room and look at your child's pupils. Switch on a bright light and watch them shrink, then switch it off and count how long they take to open up again. Ask: why does your eye do that? Never look straight at the Sun, even with sunglasses.

visual.caption: Front or back of the eye? Drag each part, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: send lamp light off a ball into an eye, label the eye, set the pupil, focus the lens on the retina and order the steps to the brain.

kid: You see a ball when light from a lamp hits it and bounces into your eyes. Your eyes take light in. They do not send light out.

Light goes in through the pupil. The pupil is a hole, not a dot. It looks black because light goes in and does not come back out. The coloured ring round it is the iris. In the dark, your pupil gets big to let more light in. In bright sun, it gets small. The iris does this by itself.
Behind the pupil is the lens. It bends the light so a sharp picture lands on the retina at the back. The picture there is upside down!
The retina sends a message along the optic nerve to your brain. Your brain works out what you see. It turns the picture the right way up.
adult: Ages 7 to 9. England's Year 6 science asks children to explain that we see things because light travels from light sources to our eyes, or from light sources to objects and then to our eyes. The parts of the eye (pupil, iris, lens, retina, optic nerve) are named in BBC Bitesize KS2 'How do we see?' and taught in full at KS3. Key words: light source, reflect, pupil, iris, lens, retina, optic nerve.

Make the path of light visible. In a dark room, shine a torch on a toy and ask where the light goes next. Draw arrows from the torch to the toy and from the toy to the eye, never from the eye outwards. Then look at each other's pupils in dim light and in bright light.

Common mistakes: thinking eyes send out rays to the things we look at (a well-documented idea in children, Driver and others, 1985); calling the pupil a black dot rather than a hole; expecting the pupil to shrink in the dark; thinking the picture forms on the lens or the pupil; and thinking the eye, not the brain, makes sense of what we see. Be careful with 'the eye sees': the eye collects light, the brain interprets it.

In the lab your child taps where light goes to see a ball and then a lamp, drags names onto a side view of the eye, picks the pupil size for a sunny beach, a dark bedroom and a classroom, makes the lens thinner for a far tree and fatter for a near book until the picture is sharp (and upside down) on the retina, and orders the five steps from pupil to brain.

practice.prompt: You look at a teddy in a lit room. Which way does the light go?
choices: From the lamp, off the teddy, into my eyes
From my eyes out to the teddy
From the teddy, which glows by itself
practice.hint: Which thing makes light? Follow the light from there.
practice.explain: The lamp makes the light. It bounces off the teddy and goes into your eyes. Eyes take light in; they do not send it out.

practice.prompt: Light goes from a lamp to a toy, then into your eye. The lamp is {a} m from the toy. The toy is {b} m from your eye. How many metres does the light travel?
practice.hint: The light goes lamp to toy, then toy to eye. Add the two parts of the trip.
practice.explain: The light travels {a} m to the toy and then {b} m to your eye: {a} + {b} = {=a+b} m.

practice.prompt: In a dark room your pupil is {a} mm wide. You step into bright sun and it gets {b} mm smaller. How wide is it now, in mm?
practice.hint: Bright light makes the pupil smaller. Take the change away from the dark-room size.
practice.explain: The pupil shrinks in bright light: {a} − {b} = {=a-b} mm. A smaller pupil lets less light in.

practice.prompt: Where does the sharp picture land inside the eye?
choices: On the retina at the back
practice.hint: The lens bends the light. Where does the bent light end up?
practice.explain: The lens bends the light so it meets on the retina at the back of the eye. That is where the picture forms.

practice.prompt: Which part carries the message from the eye to the brain?
practice.hint: It leaves the back of the eye like a cable.
practice.explain: The optic nerve carries the message from the retina to the brain. The iris and lens are at the front and work on the light.

choices: A hole that lets light in
A black dot painted on the eye
The coloured part of the eye
pool.hint: Light has to get inside the eye somehow. Where does it go in?
pool.explain: The pupil is a hole in the iris. It looks black because light goes in and does not come back out.

pool.prompt: You walk into a dark cave. What do your pupils do?
pool.hint: There is not much light in a cave. Does the eye need more or less light to get in?
pool.explain: In the dark the pupils get bigger, so more light can get into the eye.

pool.prompt: Tom says his eyes shine a beam onto the things he looks at. Is he right?
choices: No, light bounces off things into his eyes
Yes, that is how eyes work
pool.hint: Can you see anything in a room with no light at all?
pool.explain: In a room with no light you see nothing, so eyes cannot make their own light. Light from a source bounces off things into our eyes.

pool.prompt: A bike light is {a} m from a sign. Light bounces off the sign and goes {b} m to your eye. How far does the light travel in all, in metres?
pool.hint: Add the trip from the bike light to the sign and the trip from the sign to your eye.
pool.explain: {a} m to the sign and {b} m back to your eye: {a} + {b} = {=a+b} m.

choices: Bends the light so the picture is sharp
Sends the message to the brain
pool.hint: Think of a magnifying glass. What does it do to light?
pool.explain: The lens bends the light so it meets on the retina and the picture is sharp. The iris gives the eye its colour, and the optic nerve carries the message.

pool.prompt: Which part works out what you are looking at?
pool.hint: The eye catches the light. Where does the message go?
pool.explain: The eye collects the light, and the optic nerve takes the message to the brain. The brain works out what you see.

pool.prompt: Your pupils are {a} mm wide in bright sun. In a dim room they get {b} mm wider. How wide are they now, in mm?
pool.hint: In dim light the pupil opens up, so add the change.
pool.explain: Dim light makes the pupils open up: {a} + {b} = {=a+b} mm, so more light gets in.

pool.prompt: Put these in order: brain, pupil, retina, lens, optic nerve. Which comes third?
pool.hint: Light goes in through the pupil, then the lens bends it. Where does it land?
pool.explain: Pupil, lens, retina, optic nerve, brain. The retina is third: the picture lands there after the lens bends the light.

pool.prompt: Which part is the coloured ring at the front of the eye?
pool.hint: Blue, brown or green eyes: which part has the colour?
pool.explain: The iris is the coloured ring. It changes the size of the pupil in the middle.

pool.prompt: Why must you never look straight at the Sun?
choices: Its strong light can harm the retina
It makes the pupil too big
pool.hint: Which part at the back of the eye catches the light?
pool.explain: The Sun's light is so strong that it can burn the retina, even when the pupil is small. Sunglasses do not make it safe.
